# Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning

Anagha Aneesh Sebastian Ibarraran Frank Hu Jason Liu Grant M.
Rotskoff^(\*) Stanford University

###### Abstract

Automating synthesis planning for small-molecule drug design requires
chemical reasoners that are accurate as well as open to inspection and
adaptation, yet frontier language models remain unreliable at predicting
reaction outcomes and difficult to deploy, while small open-weight
models lack the necessary domain reasoning. We show that frontier
supervision can serve as a one-time bootstrap for open models on forward
reaction prediction. Our models, Resonance, distill an open-weight
teacher’s reasoning traces and then learn from their own verified
outputs, turning a small base model with near-zero accuracy into a
capable reaction predictor, while a stronger student surpasses its
teacher through distillation alone. Accuracy, however, does not bring
robust reasoning: the small student inherits its teacher’s single-pass
style, self-training mainly sharpens answers it could already reach, and
it readily abandons correct answers under pushback, suggesting that
chemical reasoning models should be evaluated on the robustness of their
reasoning as well as on the accuracy of their answers.

¹¹footnotetext: Corresponding author: Grant M. Rotskoff,
[rotskoff@stanford.edu](mailto:rotskoff@stanford.edu).

## 1 Introduction

Chemical foundation models are now widely used for molecular discovery
tasks, but designing small organic molecules for pharmaceutical
applications often requires iterative and time-consuming chemical
synthesis planning, which these models do not provide. While frontier
large language models (LLMs) have acquired substantial chemical
knowledge and reasoning ability, they are far from reliable for
predicting chemical synthesis ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)).
Furthermore, their closed weights and increasing restrictions in the
sciences make them difficult to adapt and deploy as components of
specialized workflows. Smaller open-weight models avoid these
constraints but perform poorly on domain-specific reasoning without
further training ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib39)). There is an urgent
need for robust chemical reasoners to realize automated scientific
applications.

Forward reaction prediction, predicting the major product of a chemical
reaction from its reactants, is a core problem in computer-aided
synthesis planning ([Coley et al., 2018](#bib.bib11)). Progress on this
problem supports retrosynthesis ([Gao et al., 2024](#bib.bib2);
[Genheden et al., 2020](#bib.bib3)), route scoring ([Segler et al.,
2018](#bib.bib30); [Bran et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), and autonomous
experimentation ([Boiko et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)). The task is also a
natural probe of chemical reasoning in language models because a model
must recognize which functional groups react, infer the most likely
transformation, and choose between competing products. Specialist
sequence-to-sequence models trained on reaction SMILES already predict
reaction products with high accuracy ([Schwaller et al.,
2019](#bib.bib29)), but they provide answers without explanation and
cannot be instructed or questioned. Models that reason in natural
language pair each prediction with a rationale that can be inspected and
composed into larger chemical workflows ([Bran et al., 2026](#bib.bib7);
[Boiko et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)).

One way to close this gap is to distill a frontier model’s reasoning
traces into a smaller model ([Hsieh et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)) and let
it continue learning from its own verified outputs ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib43); [Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18)). Final accuracy
establishes whether this works, but reveals little about why. It does
not show which post-training stage is responsible for improvements,
whether the answer depends on the model being trained, or how the
resulting model reasons. We study these questions by training Resonance,
a family of open-weight reasoning models for forward reaction prediction
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
A teacher, Kimi K3 ([Kimi Team, 2026](#bib.bib1)), supplies reasoning
traces for supervised fine-tuning of a student (Stage S1), which then
trains on its own verified-correct outputs through rejection-sampling
fine-tuning (Stage S2) and preference optimization (Stage S3). We train
Resonance-8B from Qwen3-8B ([Qwen-Team, 2025](#bib.bib25)) and, with
identical teacher traces, Resonance-27B from the stronger Qwen3.8-27B
([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib4)).

Our contributions are:

- •
  Resonance, open-weight reasoning models for forward reaction
  prediction and a protocol to build them by distilling a frontier
  teacher’s reasoning traces and then self-training on the student’s own
  verified outputs.
- •
  A stage-by-stage analysis of post-training, showing that self-training
  substantially improves a weak student but adds little to a stronger
  one, and that the difference can be anticipated from how much of the
  training set the student already solves.
- •
  An analysis of how the student reasons, showing that it inherits the
  reasoning style of its training traces and that its accuracy gains do
  not introduce robustness to prompting or feedback.

## 2 Related Work

Reaction prediction and LLMs for chemistry. Forward reaction prediction
is now commonly framed as translation between reactant and product
SMILES ([Weininger, 1988](#bib.bib35)), an approach popularized by the
Molecular Transformer ([Schwaller et al., 2019](#bib.bib29)), which
outperformed earlier template-based and template-free approaches ([Liu
et al., 2017](#bib.bib21); [Segler and Waller, 2017](#bib.bib15)).
Chemical language models pre-trained on large molecular corpora learn
transferable molecular representations ([Ross et al.,
2022](#bib.bib27)), and general-purpose LLMs have since been applied to
reaction prediction and other chemistry tasks ([Jablonka et al.,
2024](#bib.bib19); [Guo et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib32); [Hu et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)). Prior work adapts
general models to chemistry through continued pretraining on scientific
corpora ([Taylor et al., 2022](#bib.bib31)), instruction tuning on
curated chemistry datasets ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib44); [Bran et
al., 2025](#bib.bib20)), or reinforcement learning on verifiable
chemistry tasks ([Narayanan et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)). We instead start
from general-purpose models and add domain competence only through
post-training on the target task.

Distillation, self-distillation and preference optimization. Distilling
a teacher’s reasoning traces into a smaller student is a standard
training recipe ([Hinton et al., 2015](#bib.bib16); [Hsieh et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17)) and underpins recent open reasoning models ([Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib13)). Students can also improve on their own verified
outputs through rejection sampling fine-tuning ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib43); [Singh et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)) or iterative
self-evolution on verified trajectories ([Guan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)). Recent work frames such self-improvement as
sharpening the model’s distribution toward answers it already produces
([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)).
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) ([Rafailov et al.,
2024](#bib.bib26)) replaces the reward model with pairwise preferences
and has been applied to self-generated preferences ([Yuan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib42); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) and to pairs of
correct and incorrect reasoning chains ([Pang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib45)). We combine these steps in a single pipeline and
measure what each contributes.

Reasoning intervention. Chain of thought (CoT) explanations are not
always faithful to what drives a model’s answer ([Turpin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib46); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), and reasoning models
have less control over their traces than over their final outputs
([Yueh-Han et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). Test-time strategies help most
when a model has been trained to use them; specifically, fine-tuning on
long reasoning traces allows a model to be prompted to extend its
reasoning and improve its accuracy as a result ([Muennighoff et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)). Model improvement through self-training depends on
whether it already verifies and backtracks ([Gandhi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib47)). Without such training, models struggle to correct
their own reasoning ([Huang et al., 2023](#bib.bib33)) and tend to
change their answers when challenged ([Sharma et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23)). We study these interventions in a single scientific
domain and across successive post-training stages, asking how
distillation and self-training shape the way the resulting models reason
and respond to challenge.

## 3 Methods

Figure 1: The pipeline used to train Resonance. The teacher (Kimi K3)
generates reasoning traces, provided with the recorded product visible,
that are used to fine-tune the base model (base $`\rightarrow`$ S1). The
model is then improved on its own verified-correct traces (S1
$`\rightarrow`$ S2, rejection-sampling SFT) and its own
preference-ranked traces (S2 $`\rightarrow`$ S3, DPO) before evaluation.

### 3.1 Task formulation

We study forward reaction prediction: given reactant and reagent
molecules encoded as SMILES ([Weininger, 1988](#bib.bib35)), predict the
SMILES of the major product. We use USPTO-50k with its standard split of
40,000 training, 5,000 validation and 5,000 test reactions. Each
reaction’s reactants are split into a starting material (the first
reactant) and reagents (all other reactants). This version of the
dataset records no solvents, catalysts or conditions, so when a reaction
has a single reactant the prompt reads “Reagents: No reagents”
(Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Data, scoring and reaction classes ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

We canonicalize all molecules with RDKit ([Landrum and others,
2026](#bib.bib36)) and score a prediction as correct only if its
canonical SMILES exactly matches the canonical ground truth reaction
product (Top-1 exact match). Over $`N`$ test reactions

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathrm{Acc@1}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbbm{1}\left[\mathrm{canon}(\hat{y}_{i})=\mathrm{canon}(y_{i})\right],
``` |  |

with $`\hat{y}_{i}`$ the predicted product, $`y_{i}`$ the ground truth,
and $`\mathrm{canon}(\cdot)`$ is the RDKit canonicalization function.
The prediction is the last \<answer\> block; invalid SMILES, missing
answers and truncated generations are scored as incorrect and stay in
the denominator.

### 3.2 Base models and teacher

We start from an open-weight Qwen model, either Qwen3-8B or Qwen3.8-27B,
and elicit predictions in a CoT ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib37))
analysis followed by a delimited final SMILES answer that the scorer
extracts. The two models differ in pre-training recipe as well as size,
so we treat them as two starting points rather than as a scaling series.
We use Kimi K3 as the teacher because it is a strong open-weight model
whose traces we can release in full, so the supervision used in Stage 1
is available to anyone reproducing this work. Kimi K3, Claude Opus
5 ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib10)) and GPT-6-Astra ([OpenAI,
2026](#bib.bib48)) are also evaluated zero-shot on the test set with the
product hidden
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Generation and evaluation protocols ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Training details can be found in
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Training configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").

### 3.3 Three stages of training

Stage 1: SFT on teacher traces. We generate reasoning traces for all
40,000 training reactions with Kimi K3, showing it the starting
material, reagents and recorded product (prompt in
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
and fine-tune the Qwen model on each trace followed by the recorded
product, yielding S1. This installs the trace format and an initial
competence the small pre-trained model lacks, effectively moving the
model on-distribution for the reaction prediction task.

Stage 2: Rejection-sampling SFT on self-generated traces. We sample 8
traces per training reaction from S1, keep only those whose product is
verified as correct, and fine-tune on the retained set to yield S2. This
stage reinforces reasoning paths that actually reach correct products
and shifts the training data on-policy. For the 8B model it keeps 47,492
examples covering 19,668 reactions. Because the 27B model is already
correct on 85.8% of its S1 samples, naive rejection sampling would
mostly retrain it on solved reactions. We therefore re-balance its data
toward reactions it solves in some, but not all, of 8 traces and provide
the ground-truth product in an answer-only format for the 1,108
reactions with no correct sample (1.1% of its S2 examples;
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

Stage 3: DPO on self-generated preference pairs. We sample 16 traces per
training reaction from S2. For each reaction with at least one correct
and one incorrect sample, we take a random verified-correct trace as the
chosen response $`y_{w}`$ and the incorrect trace whose product is most
similar to the recorded product as the rejected response $`y_{l}`$,
keeping one pair per reaction. We optimize the DPO objective ([Rafailov
et al., 2024](#bib.bib26)) together with a negative log-likelihood term
on the chosen response:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{S3}}=-\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,\,y_{w},\,y_{l})}\!\left[\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_{l}\mid x)}\right)+\lambda\,\frac{1}{|y_{w}|}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)\right],
``` |  |

where $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ is the S2 checkpoint, $`\beta=0.1`$
controls regularization to the reference policy, and $`\lambda=0.2`$
weights the per-token log-likelihood of the chosen response. The
preference term uses log-probabilities summed over the response; the
likelihood term, similar to [Pang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib45), keeps the
probability of correct traces from falling during preference
optimization.

### 3.4 Reasoning analysis

We probe Resonance-8B at each stage with prompts that change how it
reasons, feedback on its answers, and repeated sampling. All probes use
the evaluation prompt and scorer, temperature $`0.6`$, Top-$`p=0.95`$,
Top-$`k=20`$, an 8,192-token output cap, and an independent seed for
each reaction, with 8 draws per reaction unless stated otherwise
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Generation and evaluation protocols ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Each condition is compared with a baseline on the same reactions, using
paired tests clustered by reaction
(Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Statistical methods ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Probe baselines differ slightly from the single-draw headline accuracies
(Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Generation and evaluation protocols ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

Reasoning-length prompts. We append an instruction asking the model to
commit to its first well-supported answer, to consider alternatives
before finalizing, or to think more before committing. These
instructions provide no chemical information. Each is compared with an
unprompted resample of the same model.

Feedback. After the model’s first answer, we send a second user turn,
regardless of that answer’s correctness: mild doubt (“there may be an
issue with it”), told wrong, marked wrong by an evaluator, or told
correct
(Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Each is compared with a neutral “review your answer” turn.

Backtracking. We count a fixed list of backtracking phrases (for example
“wait”, “let me reconsider”, “alternatively”) inside the thinking block,
frozen before any intervention was run, and report events per 1,000
output tokens and the share of traces with at least one event
(Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Measuring backtracking ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
This is a surface measure that we use only to compare conditions.

Repeated sampling. We draw nine predictions per reaction (the first
answer plus 8 resamples) and evaluate plurality voting for
$`k\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}`$ (plurality@$`k`$): the most frequent canonicalized
product among the first $`k`$ samples is selected, excluding unparsable
outputs and resolving ties by earliest occurrence. We also report
pass@$`k`$, the fraction of reactions with at least one correct
prediction among the first $`k`$ samples.

## 4 Results

Figure 2: Top-1 exact-match accuracy on the USPTO-50k test set
($`N=5{,}000`$) for Resonance-8B at each stage (base $`\rightarrow`$ S1
teacher SFT $`\rightarrow`$ S2 rejection-sampling SFT $`\rightarrow`$ S3
DPO), and for Kimi K3 (teacher, 57.4%), Claude Opus 5 (78.7%) and
GPT-6-Astra (63.0%), all three evaluated zero-shot. Each stage improves
on the previous one, and the two self-training stages together add 11.8
points without teacher supervision. Error bars are 95% Wilson intervals.

### 4.1 Self-training improves the 8B model after teacher-guided SFT

We evaluate on the 5,000-reaction test split of USPTO-50k, a standard
benchmark of roughly 50,000 reactions drawn from US patents ([Lowe,
2012](#bib.bib22); [Schneider et al., 2016](#bib.bib28)). A prediction
is evaluated as correct if its RDKit-canonical SMILES exactly matches
the recorded product. We compare Resonance-8B at each stage with its
teacher, Kimi K3, and with two frontier models, Claude Opus 5
([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib10)) and GPT-6-Astra ([OpenAI,
2026](#bib.bib48)).

Out of the box, Qwen3-8B is unable to complete this forward reaction
prediction task. It predicts 1.2% of products correctly
(Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Few-shot examples raise its format compliance to 89% of finished
generations but leave accuracy at 1–2%, and over half of its valid
answers simply copy the starting material
(Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 The base model does not fail only because of format ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Teacher SFT (S1) changes this, lifting accuracy to 31.0%. For this small
model, S1 is an essential step in establishing baseline task performance
that supports further gains via self-training. Rejection sampling (S2)
and preference optimization (S3) can only learn from the model’s
self-produced correct answers, and with the base model alone (1.2%
accuracy) there is almost nothing to learn from. After S1, the model is
able to learn from its own verified work. S2 adds 7.9 points and S3
another 3.9, reaching 42.8% accuracy overall, and each stage is a
significant improvement on the one before
(Appendix [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Stage-by-stage significance ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
More than a quarter of the total improvement (11.8 of 41.6 points)
arrives after the teacher has left the training loop. Rejection sampling
is needed: applying DPO directly to S1, without S2, recovers only about
half of this gain
(Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Is rejection-sampling SFT (S2) necessary? ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Despite these gains, the performance of the student model still lags
behind that of the teacher model. This raises the question of whether
the ceiling of student model performance is set by its pretraining
recipe or if this is an artifact of the teacher model traces.
Self-training alone cannot answer this question because it only
reinforces reaction knowledge the S1 model can already reach
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
We return to this question in
Section [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 A stronger starting point needs less of the pipeline ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"),
where the same traces are used to train a stronger model.

Figure 3: Accuracy by reaction class for Resonance-8B. (A) Student minus
teacher zero-shot accuracy (Resonance-8B minus Kimi K3) at each stage;

### 4.2 Students and teacher understand different chemistry

Aggregate accuracy hides how unevenly the student’s gains are
distributed across reaction classes (see
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Self-training improves the 8B model after teacher-guided SFT ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
and
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.1 Accuracy by class for every model and stage ‣ Appendix C Where do the students beat the teacher? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Resonance-8B trails Kimi K3 on most classes but overtakes it, by wide
margins, on deprotections, reductions, and oxidations. These three
classes expose a limitation of USPTO-50k: the dataset often omits the
reagent that drives the transformation, and the reducing, oxidizing, or
deprotecting agent is missing from most of these prompts. Given such a
prompt zero-shot, Kimi K3 typically concludes that no reaction occurs,
which is a genuine error rather than a scoring artifact
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Are the teacher’s low scores real errors? ‣ Appendix C Where do the students beat the teacher? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Yet, when generating training traces with the product provided, the same
teacher can aptly explain the transformation and transfer knowledge to
the student. The classes also respond differently to self-training
(Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Self-training improves the 8B model after teacher-guided SFT ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")B;
Table [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ C.1 Accuracy by class for every model and stage ‣ Appendix C Where do the students beat the teacher? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
For most classes, the gain comes at S2: deprotections improve the most
overall (22.0 percentage points from S1 to S3), and acylations make
almost all of their 14.5-point gain at S2. Reductions are the one large
class that improves mainly at S3, gaining 2.6 points at S2 and 9.9 at
S3. Oxidations go the other way, gaining 16.3 points at S2 and then
losing 20.0 at S3 to end below S1.

### 4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training

A common way to improve a reasoning model without further training is to
spend more compute at inference time: asking it to think more, to
consider alternatives, or to revise its answer in response to feedback.
We test these strategies naively, through prompting alone, on a model
that was never trained to use them
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Reasoning analysis ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Most do not improve Resonance-8B’s accuracy at any stage and incur a
slight performance cost. The reason appears to lie in the reasoning
style the student inherits from its training data.

#### The student inherits a single-pass reasoning style.

We measure how often a trace reconsiders its own reasoning by counting
backtracking phrases such as “wait” or “let me reconsider”
(Section [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Reasoning analysis ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Qwen3-8B backtracks in every trace, but the Kimi K3 traces it is
fine-tuned on rarely do: only 11% contain a backtracking phrase
(Table [13](#A4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ D.2 Where the student’s reasoning style comes from ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
After S1, the student matches its training data rather than its base
model, backtracking in 13% of traces, and self-training barely changes
this (15% at S3). The teacher’s traces may lack backtracking because we
asked for concise, fixed-format traces, or because the teacher could see
the product while writing them.

Figure 4: Instructions change reasoning length, not accuracy. Average
reasoning tokens against change in Top-1 accuracy relative to an
unprompted resample, for Resonance-8B at each stage, when instructed to
commit to its first supported answer, consider alternatives, or think
more. Baseline accuracy is 29.0%, 38.8% and 41.3% at S1, S2 and S3,
respectively. No instruction improves accuracy at any stage. Error bars
are $`\pm 1`$ standard error over 8 draws per reaction, clustered by
reaction.

#### Longer reasoning is not better reasoning.

Asking the model to think more produces the longest traces at every
stage (651 average tokens at S1, against 488 for an unprompted
resample), asking it to commit produces the shortest (451 tokens), and
asking it to consider alternatives falls in between
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ The student inherits a single-pass reasoning style. ‣ 4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
None of these instructions improves accuracy at any stage, and most
lower it by up to about one percentage point
(Table [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ Design. ‣ D.3 Prompts that change reasoning length ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
suggesting that pushing the model away from the way it was trained to
reason slightly reduces accuracy. Asking the model to consider
alternatives raises its backtracking about 2.4-fold (0.27 to 0.66 events
per 1,000 tokens at S1) with no gain in accuracy
(Figure [10](#A4.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Answer flips. ‣ D.4 Response to feedback ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
The student can mimic reconsidering when asked, but not constructively.

Figure 5: Sensitivity to negative feedback grows with training. Change
in Top-1 accuracy of Resonance-8B relative to a neutral “review your
answer” turn when its previous answer is returned with mild doubt, a
statement that it is wrong, a statement that an evaluator marked it
wrong, or a statement that it is correct, regardless of its actual
correctness. Baseline accuracy after the neutral review is 28.0%, 38.3%
and 41.1% at S1, S2 and S3, respectively, with 8 draws per reaction.
Negative feedback costs 3.2–3.7 points at S1 and 8.7–9.2 at S3; being
told an answer is correct is the only intervention that helps, by less
than one point. Error bars are $`\pm 1`$ standard error over 8 draws per
reaction, clustered by reaction.

#### Pushback, not evidence, changes the model’s answer.

We next return the model’s previous answer to it with feedback attached,
regardless of whether that answer was correct
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Longer reasoning is not better reasoning. ‣ 4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Because the feedback carries no information about the reaction, an ideal
model would ignore it. Being told an answer is correct is the only
intervention that asks the model to behave according to its training and
is the only one that improves performance. Negative feedback, however,
is costly. When told that its answer is wrong, the model loses 3.7
points at S1, 4.1 at S2 and 9.2 at S3; told that an evaluator marked it
wrong, it loses 3.2, 3.7 and 8.7
(Table [15](#A4.T15 "Table 15 ‣ Design. ‣ D.4 Response to feedback ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Even a mild suggestion that the answer may contain an error costs more
as training proceeds, rising from 0.3 to 0.7 to 2.1 points. The loss is
not simply a consequence of S3 having more correct answers to lose: as a
percentage of baseline accuracy, the told wrong loss is 13% at S1 and
11% at S2 but 22% at S3. Separating the two directions of change shows
what the model does with the feedback
(Table [16](#A4.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Answer flips. ‣ D.4 Response to feedback ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Told that it is wrong, the model abandons 22–32% of its initially
correct answers, against 3–6% after a neutral review, yet rescues only
about 6% of its initially incorrect ones. It treats negative feedback as
an instruction to change its answer rather than as evidence to weigh, a
form of sycophancy ([Sharma et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)), and training
does not remove this behavior at any stage.

Figure 6: Self-training sharpens answers the model could already reach.
Plurality@$`k`$ accuracy (the most frequent product among $`k`$ samples)
for Resonance-8B by reaction class and stage. Voting over nine S1
samples matches or exceeds single-sample S3 accuracy in 8 of the 10
classes with at least 40 test reactions; heterocycle formation remains
unsolved at every $`k`$. Classes follow
Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Reaction classes. ‣ A.1 Data, scoring and reaction classes ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").

#### Self-training sharpens what the model could already find.

Finally, we sample each reaction nine times to ask whether self-training
teaches the model new reactions or makes it more reliable on reactions
it could already solve
(Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Pushback, not evidence, changes the model’s answer. ‣ 4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning");
Appendix [D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Sampling several answers per reaction ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Between S1 and S3, single-sample accuracy rises by about 13 percentage
points, but the share of reactions solved in at least one of nine
samples rises by only about 4. In most reaction classes, a plurality
vote over nine S1 samples already matches or exceeds a single S3 sample.
Self-training therefore sharpens the model’s distribution toward answers
it can already reach rather than teaching it new ones ([Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)), which is why its gains in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Self-training improves the 8B model after teacher-guided SFT ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
are real but bounded. Heterocycle formation, where the 8B model almost
never samples a correct product, shows this limit most clearly. The
sharpening is also incomplete because plurality voting still improves S3
accuracy substantially, and this gain is available at inference time
without further training.

### 4.4 A stronger starting point needs less of the pipeline

We apply the same pipeline, with the same teacher traces, to
Qwen3.8-27B. Teacher SFT alone takes this model from 26.3% to 79.0%,
well above Kimi K3, whose traces it was trained on
(Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.4 A stronger starting point needs less of the pipeline ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning");
stage-level accuracies are in Appendix
Figure [8](#A2.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ B.5 Accuracy by stage for Resonance-27B ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
which answers the question left open in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Self-training improves the 8B model after teacher-guided SFT ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"):
the teacher’s traces contain more than the 8B model learns from them, so
the 8B model’s ceiling is set by pre-training rather than by its
supervision. The same holds within reaction classes, since heterocycle
formation, which the 8B model never learns, reaches 42.7% on
Resonance-27B after S1 on identical traces, and part of the 27B
student’s margin over its teacher comes from the traces themselves
rather than from the recorded products alone
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Students and teacher understand different chemistry ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
After S1 the model is also comparable to Claude Opus 5 (78.7%), although
the student is trained on USPTO-50k while Opus 5 is evaluated zero-shot.

Figure 7: Accuracy by reaction class for Resonance-27B. Bars show the
base model, S1, S2, S3, DPO applied directly to S1 (skip-S2); Kimi K3
and Claude Opus 5 (zero-shot). Teacher SFT supplies nearly all of the
gain in every class, and the later stages change accuracy by amounts
within sampling noise. Opus 5 leads on heterocycle formation, while the
student leads on reductions and oxidations, where the prompt usually
names no reagent. Classes follow
Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Reaction classes. ‣ A.1 Data, scoring and reaction classes ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").

Neither self-training stage adds measurable accuracy to Resonance-27B:
S2 reaches 79.3% and S3 79.6%, differences too small to distinguish from
sampling noise, and skipping S2 gives the same result
(Appendices [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Is rejection-sampling SFT (S2) necessary? ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
and [B.4](#A2.SS4 "B.4 Stage-by-stage significance ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Heterocycle formation rises from 42.7% to 48.5% across these stages, but
with only 103 test reactions this change is also within noise.
Self-training has little to learn from once the 27B model has been
distilled, since after S1 it already answers most of its training
reactions correctly (85.8% of samples, against 16.6% for the 8B model;
Table [7](#A2.T7 "Table 7 ‣ How much is left to learn after S1. ‣ B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"))
and few reactions yield the mix of correct and incorrect samples that
rejection sampling and preference optimization need. We rebalanced its
S2 data toward reactions it solves only some of the time to give
self-training its best chance, choosing the recipe after several
variants
(Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
but it still adds no measurable accuracy. What S1 does provide the 27B
model, in part, is concision: before training, fewer than half of its
generations reach an answer within the token budget, whereas after
fine-tuning on the teacher’s short, single-pass traces it answers within
a few hundred tokens. For this model, the reasoning style that limits
the 8B student’s robustness
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"))
may therefore be part of what makes it effective.

## 5 Conclusions

Our distillation and self-training pipeline transforms a small
open-weight model that cannot perform forward reaction prediction into a
capable one using a modest, task-specific dataset. This approach matters
as agentic methods increasingly rely on systems of many small models
([Belcak et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)), which in scientific domains must
often be specialized with far less data than general-purpose
pre-training provides ([Van Herck et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)). How much
each stage contributes, however, depends on the student. Qwen3-8B needs
teacher SFT to begin the task at all, and self-training then adds
substantially more without further supervision, whereas Qwen3.8-27B
surpasses its teacher after SFT alone and gains nothing measurable from
the later stages. Because self-training helps only while the distilled
model still fails on much of its training set, and that failure rate can
be measured after S1, it offers a practical guide to whether further
post-training is worth the cost. Benchmark accuracy, however, does not
show how these models reason. The 8B student inherits the single-pass
style of its training traces, so prompts to reason longer or consider
alternatives do not help, and self-training mainly sharpens answers the
model could already reach by plurality vote. When told a correct answer
is wrong, the student abandons 22–32% of such answers at every stage,
and the accuracy lost under pushback more than doubles between S1 and
S3. We hypothesize that the missing capability is meta-reasoning,
knowing when and how to revise: the training corpus rarely demonstrates
revision
(Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Where the student’s reasoning style comes from ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
prompted deliberation raises the surface markers of reconsidering
without raising accuracy
(Appendices [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Prompts that change reasoning length ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
and [D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Do structure changes within a trace reach the right product? ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")),
and negative feedback flips answers rather than prompting a check
(Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Response to feedback ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
These observations are consistent with the hypothesis but do not
establish it, and they suggest that models intended to reason about
chemistry should be evaluated on the robustness of their reasoning as
well as on whether they reach the correct product.

#### Limitations.

The students are trained on USPTO-50k while the frontier models are
evaluated zero-shot, so comparisons with them measure what task-specific
post-training adds rather than general chemical ability. USPTO-50k often
omits the reagent that drives a reaction, so part of what a trained
model learns is how the dataset records such reactions, and zero-shot
models are penalized for declining to infer a missing reagent. We
evaluate a single task and benchmark, train each configuration once, and
score only the final product without assessing reasoning traces for
accuracy beyond the ground truth. Finally, our reasoning analysis covers
only the 8B model, and its backtracking measure is a lexical count not
yet validated against human labels.

#### Future work.

Testing the meta-reasoning hypothesis requires training data that
demonstrates revision directly, such as failed synthetic pathways, a
diagnosis of why each failed, and recovery from them; a strong benchmark
score does not certify a teacher as a source of such data. Repeating the
reasoning analysis on the 27B model would show whether a stronger
student responds differently to feedback, and evaluating on reaction
data that records full conditions would separate chemical reasoning from
learning dataset conventions. For capable students that already solve
most of their training set, self-training will need new signal, for
example from harder or out-of-distribution chemistry, and scoring
intermediate mechanistic steps rather than only the final product would
bring evaluation closer to the reasoning these models are meant to
perform.

## Appendix A Experimental setup

### A.1 Data, scoring and reaction classes

#### Dataset.

USPTO-50k ([Schneider et al., 2016](#bib.bib28)), standard split: 40,000
train, 5,000 validation and 5,000 test reactions. All 40,000 training
reactions are used for S1. Each reaction’s reactants are split into a
*starting material* (the first reactant) and *reagents* (all other
reactants, joined with “.”). This version of the dataset records no
solvents, catalysts or conditions, so the “reagents” are in fact
co-reactants; when a reaction has a single reactant the prompt reads
“Reagents: No reagents” (1,439 of 5,000 test prompts, 28.8%). The source
files contain no atom maps; the scorers strip any that appear.

#### Scoring.

The prediction is the last \<answer\> block. Prediction and reference
are canonicalized with RDKit (isomeric SMILES, atom maps removed) and a
prediction is correct only on exact string match. The whole
dot-separated answer is canonicalized as one molecule, so fragment order
does not matter but every fragment, including counter-ions, must match;
no gold product in train or test contains more than one component.
Invalid SMILES, missing answer tags and truncated generations with no
answer are scored as incorrect and stay in the denominator
($`N=5{,}000`$). The last \<answer\> tag anywhere in the response
counts, including one inside a thinking block that never closed; a
generation truncated before any answer tag is incorrect. One scorer is
used for every model. *Sensitivity to this rule.* A stricter rule that
reads only text after a closing \</think\> tag leaves every trained 27B
checkpoint unchanged (S1/S2/S3 79.0/79.3/79.6%, skip-S2 78.8%) and the
8B base model unchanged (1.2%), but lowers the 27B base model from 26.3%
to 22.8% and the 8B students from 31.0 / 38.9 / 42.8% to 26.2 / 34.5 /
34.9% at S1/S2/S3 (skip-S2: 37.1 to 31.5%). These are not truncations:
at most one headline response per stage exceeds 8,192 tokens. The model
states its answer and does not close the thinking block, which S3 does
in 18.5% of responses (S1 16.4%, S2 10.5%). Under the stricter rule
S1$`\to`$S2 remains significant ($`+8.3`$ \[6.9, 9.8\], $`p<10^{-28}`$)
and skip-S2 remains below the full pipeline ($`-3.5`$ \[$`-4.8`$,
$`-2.1`$\], $`p<10^{-6}`$), but S2$`\to`$S3 does not ($`+0.4`$
\[$`-1.0`$, 1.8\], $`p=0.58`$).

#### Reaction classes.

We use one labeling scheme throughout the paper
(Table [2](#A1.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Reaction classes. ‣ A.1 Data, scoring and reaction classes ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
Labels come from a rule-based classifier that finds the formed bond from
functional-group and ring changes between the reactant union and the
product, followed by a per-fragment maximum common substructure search;
its class distribution on USPTO-50k is within about 1–3 points of the
published Schneider et al. distribution. Reactions that match no rule
are labeled unclassified (184 test, 1,684 training reactions). This is
not a chemical class: most are single-reactant transformations the rules
do not encode, including aryl methyl ether cleavage, N-debenzylation,
and smaller groups such as thiourea formation and MOM removal. We then
correct one systematic error on the test set: benzyl ethers
\[OX2;H0\]Cc1ccccc1) had been treated as protecting groups, which moves
282 of 5,000 test reactions (most often deprotections $`\to`$ acylation,
148, and protections $`\to`$ reductions, 34) and 2,247 of 40,000
training reactions.

### A.2 Training configurations

Both models start from open-weight Qwen checkpoints (Qwen3-8B,
Qwen3.8-27B).
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ A.2 Training configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
gives all three stages side by side so the differences between the two
models are visible. The reason S2 differs for 27B is given in
App. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").
All runs use bfloat16, gradient checkpointing and seed 42. Both S1 runs
compute the loss on all non-padding tokens, including the prompt. S2
computes it on the full sequence for 8B and on the assistant completion
only for 27B; S3 masks the prompt.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | S1 (teacher SFT) |  | S2 (RS-SFT) |  | S3 (DPO) |  |
| Parameter | 8B | 27B | 8B | 27B | 8B | 27B |
| Fine-tuning | full | full (text) | full | LoRA | LoRA | LoRA |
| Epochs / steps | 3 ep (3,750 st) | 3 ep (3,750 st) | 3 ep (2,229 st) | 1 ep (3,086 st) | 3,000 st (3.3 ep) | 1 ep (378 st) |
| Learning rate | $`2\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | $`2\!\times\!10^{-5}`$ | $`\mathbf{1\!\times\!10^{-5}}`$ | $`\mathbf{2\!\times\!10^{-5}}`$ | $`2\!\times\!10^{-6}`$ | $`2\!\times\!10^{-6}`$ |
| Warmup steps | 100 | 100 | 50 | 50 | 0 | 0 |
| Effective batch | 32 | 32 | 64 | 32 | 32 pairs | 32 pairs |
| Max sequence length | 2,048 | 4,096 | 1,024 | 2,048 | 4,096 | 4,096 |
| LoRA rank / $`\alpha`$ / dropout | – | – | – | 128 / 32 / 0.05 | 128 / 32 / 0.05 | 128 / 32 / 0.05 |
| DPO $`\beta`$; DPO:NLL | – | – | – | – | 0.1; 1.0:0.2 | 0.1; 1.0:0.2 |
| Training examples | 40,000 | 40,000 | 47,492 | 98,731 | 28,747 pairs | 12,079 pairs |
| Gold-answer fallbacks | – | – | none | 1,108 | – | – |
| GPUs | 8$`\times`$H100 | 8$`\times`$H200 | 8$`\times`$H100 | 8$`\times`$H200 | 8$`\times`$H100 | 8$`\times`$H200 |
| GPU-hours (training) | 79.8 | 41.6 | 46.3 | 31.9 | 20.4 | 4.5 |

Table 3: Training configuration by model and stage. Differences between
the models are in bold.

#### S1 data.

40,000 Kimi K3 traces for the USPTO-50k training reactions, generated on
a self-hosted endpoint with reasoning effort “low” and an 8,192-token
limit (14.6M input and 26.5M output tokens, including hidden reasoning).
The teacher sees the starting material, reagents, conditions (“NA” for
every reaction) and the recorded product, with no reaction identifiers
(prompt in
App. [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
The student is trained on the teacher’s returned content (not its
internal reasoning field) inside the thinking block, followed by the
recorded product in \<answer\> tags.

#### S2 data.

*8B:* 8 samples per training reaction from S1 (320,000 samples). All
finished, exactly correct samples of at most 1,024 tokens are kept:
47,492 examples covering 19,668 reactions (5,691 correct samples are
dropped as too long); no gold fallbacks. *27B:* see
App. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model ‣ Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").

#### S3 data.

16 samples per training reaction from S2 (T $`=`$ 0.7, 8,192 new
tokens). For each reaction with at least one correct and one incorrect
sample, one correct sample is chosen at random and paired with the
incorrect sample most similar to the target (Tanimoto similarity on
2,048-bit Morgan fingerprints, radius 2; invalid SMILES get similarity
0). Reactions without such a pair are dropped. For 27B, unfinished
samples and sequences over 4,096 tokens are removed before pairing (28
removed); for 8B no such filter is applied (an unfinished sample counts
as incorrect, and DPO truncates to 4,096 tokens). One pair is kept per
reaction: 28,747 of 40,000 reactions (71.9%) yield a pair for 8B and
12,079 (30.2%) for 27B.

#### Compute.

Training GPU-hours are in
Table [3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ A.2 Training configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning").
Sampling for S2 took about 4.2 H100-hours (8B) and 37.6 H200-hours
(27B); sampling for S3 took at most about 8 H100-hours for 8B and 60
H100-hours for 27B.

### A.3 Generation and evaluation protocols

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | S2 data | S3 data | Evaluation |
| Sampling model | S1 | S2 | each checkpoint |
| Samples per prompt | 8 | 16 | 1 (8 for §[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning") probes) |
| Temperature | 0.9 | 0.7 | 0.6 (base 8B: 0, greedy) |
| Top-$`p`$ / top-$`k`$ | 0.95 / 20 | 0.95 / 20 | 0.95 / 20 |
| Max new tokens | 1,024 | 8,192 | 16,384 (8,192 for probes) |
| Context length | 2,048 | 16,384 (8B) / 10,240 (27B) | 16,384 (8B) / 20,480 (27B) |
| Seed, 27B | $`42+i`$ | $`42+i`$ | $`42+i`$ for test row $`i`$ |
| Seed, 8B | none | none | fixed 42 (S1, S3); none (S2); $`42+i`$ (probes) |
| Thinking enabled | yes | yes | yes |

Table 4: Sampling settings. Seeds: “fixed” means the same seed on every
request.

#### Frontier models.

Kimi K3, Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6-Astra are evaluated zero-shot on the
same 5,000 test reactions with the evaluation prompt in
App. [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
(short system prompt), one sample each, 16,384 maximum output tokens
(for GPT-6-Astra this limit includes hidden reasoning). *Kimi K3*
(moonshotai/Kimi-K3, self-hosted endpoint, reasoning enabled at effort
“low”; completed 2026-09-16): 57.4%. *Claude Opus 5* (claude-opus-5,
Anthropic API, adaptive thinking, provider-default sampling since the
API rejects a temperature; 2026-08-10 to 2026-09-12): 78.7%.
*GPT-6-Astra* (gpt-6-astra, OpenAI API, default reasoning effort and
sampling; 2026-09-11/12): 63.0%. No request is missing from any run;
responses with no parsable answer (9 for Opus 5, 0 for the others) count
as incorrect.

#### Why the probe baselines differ from the headline numbers.

The
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
probes sample each 8B checkpoint eight times per reaction at test time,
whereas the headline accuracies in
Figure [2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
use a single sample, so their baseline accuracies differ slightly.

### A.4 Prompts

#### Teacher trace generation (S1 data).

Empty reagent fields are rendered as “None specified”.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SYSTEM: You are an expert organic chemist with deep knowledge of
reaction

mechanisms, reagent roles, and synthetic strategy. Given a reaction
described

by SMILES strings, generate a clear, structured reaction trace that
would be

useful as training data for a chemistry AI agent focused on
retrosynthesis and

forward prediction.

USER:

Starting Material: {starting_material}

Reagents: {reagents}

Reaction Conditions: {conditions}

Product: {product}

Write a reaction trace covering:

1. \*\*Reaction type\*\*: Name and classify this reaction (e.g. Suzuki
coupling,

reductive amination).

2. \*\*Transformation\*\*: Which bonds are broken and which are formed;
how the

carbon skeleton changes.

3. \*\*Mechanism\*\*: Step-by-step electron-pushing mechanism (concise
but

chemically precise).

4. \*\*Reagent roles\*\*: What each reagent/condition does and why it is
necessary.

5. \*\*Retrosynthetic note\*\*: The retrosynthetic disconnection that
reveals this

as the key step.

Use standard organic chemistry terminology. Be concise -- aim for
150-300 words.

#### S1 training target.

The S1 training prompt is shorter than the evaluation prompt (it has no
instruction block). The same text is used for both models.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SYSTEM: You are an expert organic chemist specializing in the forward

prediction of organic reactions. Your task is to predict the major
product of

organic reactions given starting materials and reagents. Return the
answer

between \<answer\> and \</answer\> tags.

USER: Here are the SMILES of the starting material and reagent(s).

Starting material: {starting_material}

Reagents: {reagents}

ASSISTANT: \<think\>

{Kimi K3 trace}

\</think\>

\<answer\>

{recorded product}

\</answer\>

#### Example teacher trace.

Patent US20120114765A1, class “acylation” (an amide coupling); the
teacher used 550 output tokens, including hidden reasoning. The teacher
receives the filled user turn below; the trace it returns is copied
verbatim into the thinking block of the S1 training example, and the
recorded product is the answer. Neither text has been edited.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

TEACHER INPUT (user turn; system prompt and instructions as above):

Starting Material: O=C(O)c1cc(\[N+\](=O)\[O-\])c(Sc2c(Cl)cncc2Cl)s1

Reagents: Nc1cccc2cnccc12

Reaction Conditions: NA

Product: O=C(Nc1cccc2cnccc12)c1cc(\[N+\](=O)\[O-\])c(Sc2c(Cl)cncc2Cl)s1

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SYSTEM: You are an expert organic chemist specializing in the forward

prediction of organic reactions. Your task is to predict the major
product of

organic reactions given starting materials and reagents. Return the
answer

between \<answer\> and \</answer\> tags.

USER: Here are the SMILES of the starting material and reagent(s).

Starting material: O=C(O)c1cc(\[N+\](=O)\[O-\])c(Sc2c(Cl)cncc2Cl)s1

Reagents: Nc1cccc2cnccc12

ASSISTANT: \<think\>

\## Reaction Trace

\*\*1. Reaction type:\*\* Amide bond formation (peptide-type coupling) —
a carboxylic acid is condensed with a primary aromatic amine
(5-aminoisoquinoline) to give a carboxamide. Classified as a
nucleophilic acyl substitution / condensation.

\*\*2. Transformation:\*\*

- \*\*Broken:\*\* The C–OH bond of the thiophene carboxylic acid (the
–OH is lost); one N–H bond of the aminoisoquinoline.

- \*\*Formed:\*\* A new C(=O)–N amide bond linking the thiophene
carbonyl carbon to the isoquinoline nitrogen. Net loss of H₂O.

- The carbon skeleton is unchanged; the nitro, chloro, and thioether
(S-linked dichloropyridine) substituents on the thiophene are
spectators.

\*\*3. Mechanism:\*\*

1. The carboxylic acid is activated (in situ by a coupling reagent or
via prior conversion to an acid chloride/active ester), making the
carbonyl more electrophilic.

2. The lone pair of the aniline-type nitrogen attacks the carbonyl
carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate (zwitterionic alkoxide).

3. Proton transfer neutralizes the intermediate.

4. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate: the C–O bond of the leaving
group breaks, the carbonyl reforms, and the activated oxygen group (or
OH after activation) departs.

5. Deprotonation of the ammonium nitrogen furnishes the neutral amide.

\*\*4. Reagent roles:\*\*

- \*\*5-Aminoisoquinoline:\*\* nucleophilic coupling partner; its ring
nitrogen (aromatic amine) attacks the acyl carbon. Used because the
target amide bears this heteroaryl group.

- \*\*Coupling conditions (implied, e.g., EDC/HOBt, SOCl₂, or HATU):\*\*
convert the unreactive –OH into a good leaving group; carboxylic acids
and amines alone only form a salt and do not condense.

\*\*5. Retrosynthetic note:\*\* Disconnect the C(=O)–N amide bond — the
classic amide disconnection. This reveals the thiophene carboxylic acid
(acyl synthon) plus 5-aminoisoquinoline (amine synthon), identifying
amide coupling as the final key step after the thioether-linked
nitrothiophene core is assembled.

\</think\>

\<answer\>

O=C(Nc1cccc2cnccc12)c1cc(\[N+\](=O)\[O-\])c(Sc2c(Cl)cncc2Cl)s1

\</answer\>

The trace contains one chemical error that is kept in the training data:
under reagent roles it says the ring nitrogen of 5-aminoisoquinoline
attacks the acyl carbon. The nucleophile is the exocyclic amino group;
the product SMILES and the rest of the trace show this correctly.

#### Evaluation prompt.

The user turn is identical for all models and stages. Two system prompts
were used: the short one for the 8B students (all stages and all
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
probes) and for the three frontier models; the long one for the 8B base
model, every 27B evaluation (base, S1, S2, S3) and the 8B S2- and
S3-data sampling.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

USER:

Here are the SMILES of the starting material and reagent(s).

Starting material: {starting_material}

Reagents: {reagent_list}

Predict the single most likely primary product of the chemical reaction
in

SMILES format.

The reaction should be chemically reasonable, following typical organic

reactivity principles.

Instructions:

 1. Identify the functional groups in the starting material

2. Determine which reagent(s) will react with these functional groups

3. Apply your knowledge of organic reaction mechanisms to predict the
major

product

4. Consider regioselectivity and stereoselectivity where applicable

If your proposed mechanism or product seems chemically implausible,
revise

your reasoning and try a different mechanistic path.

Return the answer between \<answer\> and \</answer\> tags.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,U1lTVEVNIChzaG9ydCk6CllvdSBhcmUgYW4gZXhwZXJ0IG9yZ2FuaWMgY2hlbWlzdCBzcGVjaWFsaXppbmcgaW4gdGhlIGZvcndhcmQgcHJlZGljdGlvbiBvZgpvcmdhbmljIHJlYWN0aW9ucy4KWW91ciB0YXNrIGlzIHRvIHByZWRpY3QgdGhlIG1ham9yIHByb2R1Y3QocykKb2Ygb3JnYW5pYyByZWFjdGlvbnMgZ2l2ZW4gc3RhcnRpbmcgbWF0ZXJpYWxzIGFuZCByZWFnZW50cy4=)

SYSTEM (short):

You are an expert organic chemist specializing in the forward prediction
of

organic reactions.

Your task is to predict the major product(s)

of organic reactions given starting materials and reagents.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

SYSTEM (long):

You are an expert organic chemist specializing in the forward prediction
of

organic reactions.

Correctly predicting the product of an organic reaction involves
understanding

of several key concepts.

Some of the most important concepts to consider include:

1. Acid-base chemistry: these reactions will proceed from a stronger
acid to a

weaker one.

2. Single displacement reactions: Similarly, these reactions will
proceed by a

more reactive element displacing a less reactive one.

3. Redox reactions: identify the relationship between reagents and their

potential for reducing/oxidizing specific functional groups on a
molecule.

4. Mechanistic analysis: leveraging knowledge of common reaction
mechanisms,

one can infer key functional groups in a molecule and their potential

relationships to reagents and other key intramolecular functional groups

Your task is to predict the major product(s)

of organic reactions given starting materials and reagents.

#### Reasoning-length prompts (§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

Each is appended to the evaluation prompt after a blank line; the
control is an unmodified resample.

- •
  Commit: Reason directly to the answer. Commit to your first
  well-supported conclusion and do not revisit earlier steps or explore
  alternatives.
- •
  Consider alternatives: Before finalizing, consider at least two
  plausible product hypotheses and actively check whether any earlier
  inference could be wrong. Revise if a better interpretation is
  available.
- •
  Think more: Work through this carefully and at length: consider the
  plausible reaction pathways before committing, and check your proposed
  product against the starting material and reagents.

#### Feedback prompts (§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

Sent as a second user turn after the model’s first answer, whatever that
answer was.

- •
  Neutral review (baseline): Review your work above. If you would keep
  your answer, restate it; if you would change it, give the revised
  answer instead. Either way, put your final answer between \<answer\>
  and \</answer\> tags.
- •
  Mild doubt: Please double-check the answer above; there may be an
  issue with it. Put your final answer between \<answer\> and
  \</answer\> tags.
- •
  Told wrong: Your answer above is incorrect. Work out where the
  reasoning went wrong and give the correct product. Put your final
  answer between \<answer\> and \</answer\> tags.
- •
  Marked wrong (authority): An evaluator marked the answer above as
  incorrect. Revise it accordingly and give the correct product. Put
  your final answer between \<answer\> and \</answer\> tags.
- •
  Told correct: Your answer above is correct. Verify it and return the
  final answer. Put your final answer between \<answer\> and \</answer\>
  tags.

#### What the model sees in the second turn.

The conversation is \[system, task, first response, feedback\]. The
Qwen3 chat template removes the thinking block from earlier assistant
turns, so in every feedback condition the model sees only its previous
final answer, not its reasoning trace.

The number of available preference pairs does not explain the 8B result:

### B.3 Why S2 was rebalanced for the 27B model

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### How much is left to learn after S1.

|                                             |               |                |
|---------------------------------------------|---------------|----------------|
|                                             | Qwen3-8B S1   | Qwen3.8-27B S1 |
| Training-set accuracy, per sample (%)       | 16.6          | 85.8           |
| Reactions with $`\geq`$1 correct sample (%) | 51.8          | 97.2           |
| Reactions with all 8 correct (%)            | 0.3 (116)     | 65.5 (26,197)  |
| Reactions with 1–7 correct (“mixed”, %)     | 51.5 (20,588) | 31.7 (12,695)  |
| Reactions with 0 correct (%)                | 48.2 (19,296) | 2.8 (1,108)    |

Table 7: Training-set difficulty after S1 (8 samples per training
reaction; S2-data sampling settings of
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.3 Generation and evaluation protocols ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
A sample counts as correct if it is exactly correct, before any length
filter.

For 8B, the 1,024-token filter lowers the share of reactions with a
usable correct sample from 51.8% to 49.2% (19,668). For 27B every
correct sample fits the 2,048-token bound. The 8B training-set accuracy
(16.6%) is below its test accuracy (31.0%) because S2 data are sampled
at $`T=0.9`$ with a 1,024-token cap.

#### 27B S2 construction.

For reactions with 1–7 usable correct samples, all are kept (65,082
examples). For reactions with 8 of 8 correct, one sample is kept, plus a
second for a random subset (32,541 “easy replay” examples; 2:1 mixed to
easy). For the 1,108 reactions with no correct sample, the recorded
product is given as an answer-only target. Total: 98,731 examples (98.9M
tokens) covering all 40,000 reactions. The gold fallbacks are
supervision from the dataset labels, not self-generated; they are 1.1%
of S2 examples.

#### Recipe selection.

The 27B S2 recipe was chosen after several variants. One earlier variant
(LoRA, 3 epochs, 19,096 examples, one shortest correct trace per
reaction with upsampling of weak classes) was evaluated on the test set
(78.2%) before the final recipe was fixed. The final recipe uses
rank-128 LoRA (the same adapter configuration as S3) for one epoch
because full fine-tuning is expensive at this scale: a full fine-tuning
run on all 274,658 correct samples ran at about 0.21 epochs per 5 hours
on 8$`\times`$H200 (about 73 hours for 3 epochs), whereas LoRA processed
about 2.3$`\times`$ more examples per second (7.1 vs. 3.1) and one epoch
of the final difficulty-mixed dataset (98,731 examples) took 4.0 hours.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning is the standard way to adapt models of
this size.

#### The adapter changes the model.

Although S1 and S2 have almost the same accuracy, 345 test reactions
(6.9%) change outcome between them: 181 become correct and 164 become
incorrect.

#### Base-model knowledge.

Before any training, Qwen3.8-27B reaches 26.3% top-1. Only 40.8% of its
generations close their thinking block within 16,384 tokens; on those it
is 54.2% accurate (1,105 of 2,039), and a further 209 correct answers
are stated inside unfinished thinking.

## Appendix D How does the student reason?

### D.1 Measuring backtracking

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Lexicon.

We count case-insensitive, word-bounded matches of a fixed list of
phrases inside the thinking block only. The list was frozen (definition
2026-09-12.1) before any intervention was generated:

- •
  *Reversal:* wait; hold on; hmm; oops; scratch that; that/this/the
  above is (or was, would be) wrong/incorrect/not right/a mistake; I
  made a mistake/error; no, that is wrong; I was wrong/mistaken; on
  second thought; actually.
- •
  *Revision:* instead (of); rather than; let me re-…/try again/start
  over/redo/rethink/reconsider/revisit; reconsider(ing);
  revise/revising/revised/revision; correction; on closer/further
  inspection/reflection/thought; going back; back up; reverse/reversing.
- •
  *Branching:* alternatively; another
  possibility/option/route/candidate/way; other possibilities/options; a
  second possibility/option; option b–z; could also be; might also be;
  or it could/might be; two possibilities; both are/seem plausible; on
  the other hand.
- •
  *Markers:* \<candidate\>, \<reconsideration\>, \<revision\>,
  \<alternative\> tags.

Rates are reported as events per 1,000 output tokens (the whole
generation, counted with the Qwen3-8B tokenizer; for the Kimi K3 corpus,
the trace text) and as the share of traces with at least one event.
“Wait” accounts for 87% of reversal matches; we also computed every rate
without it.

The corpus’s lack of backtracking has at least two possible causes: the
teacher saw the recorded product, and the generation prompt asked for a

(App. [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Prompts ‣ Appendix A Experimental setup ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).
We do not separate these.

### D.3 Prompts that change reasoning length

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Design.

Each prompted condition is paired with an unprompted resample of the
same model on the same 5,000 reactions, 8 draws per reaction, with
independent per-reaction seeds (per-draw accuracies are consistent with
independent draws, $`\chi^{2}`$ $`p=0.26`$–$`1.00`$). The per-reaction
mean difference is tested across reactions
(App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Statistical methods ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")).

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Prompt | S1 | S2 | S3 |
| Default (resample) | 0  \[488\] | 0  \[469\] | 0  \[475\] |
| Commit to first answer | $`-1.03`$ ($`p<0.001`$) \[451\] | $`-0.82`$ ($`p<0.001`$) \[432\] | $`-0.49`$ ($`p=0.026`$) \[437\] |
| Consider alternatives | $`+0.14`$ ($`p=0.56`$) \[516\] | $`-0.69`$ ($`p=0.003`$) \[496\] | $`-0.46`$ ($`p=0.042`$) \[505\] |
| Think more | $`-0.90`$ ($`p<0.001`$) \[651\] | $`-0.26`$ ($`p=0.28`$) \[608\] | $`-0.42`$ ($`p=0.062`$) \[612\] |

Table 14: Change in top-1 accuracy (points) vs. unprompted resample,
with $`p`$-values. Baseline accuracy S1/S2/S3: 29.0 / 38.8 / 41.3%. Mean
reasoning tokens in brackets.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Across the 9 cells, 6 are significantly negative at $`p<0.05`$ and none
is significantly positive. Under a Holm–Bonferroni correction at
$`\alpha=0.05`$, 4 remain significant: S1 commit
($`p=2.4\times 10^{-5}`$), S1 think more ($`2.4\times 10^{-4}`$), S2
commit ($`2.5\times 10^{-4}`$) and S2 consider ($`2.7\times 10^{-3}`$);
the next smallest, S3 commit ($`p=0.026`$), exceeds its threshold of
$`0.05/5`$.

#### Format failures versus chemistry.

At S1, the losses under “commit” and “think more” come from answers that
fail to parse. Restricted to parsable answers, S1 commit is $`+0.98`$
($`p=0.07`$) and S1 think more is $`+1.15`$ ($`p=0.038`$), while S1
consider is $`-1.02`$ ($`p=0.052`$). At S2 and S3 the differences stay
negative or non-significant.

second turn), so that the effect of the neutral review itself is

incorrect. I$`\to`$C: share of initially incorrect answers that end
correct. A fresh resample is the no-feedback reference.

A second turn is far more stable than an independent resample. Relative
to the neutral review, “told wrong” raises C$`\to`$I about 5-fold at S1
and about 9-fold at S3, which is the direct measure of the growing
fragility.

Figure 10: Prompts raise backtracking without raising accuracy. Change
in accuracy against backtracking events per 1k output tokens for (a)
reasoning-length prompts and (b) feedback prompts, by stage. “Consider
alternatives” raises backtracking about 2.4$`\times`$ (0.27$`\to`$0.66
per 1k at S1) with no accuracy gain; “told wrong” raises it
8–18$`\times`$ over the default resample (3.5–4.1$`\times`$ over the
neutral review) and produces the largest losses.

#### What backtracking does not explain.

Across stages, the size of the “told wrong” loss does not track the
amount of backtracking: S3 loses the most accuracy while backtracking
less than S1 (3.3 vs. 4.9 events per 1k). Backtracking counts are
therefore consistent with “more reconsidering does not help”, but they
do not explain why S3 is the most fragile; the flip rates
(Table [16](#A4.T16 "Table 16 ‣ Answer flips. ‣ D.4 Response to feedback ‣ Appendix D How does the student reason? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"))
are the more direct measure.

### D.5 Do structure changes within a trace reach the right product?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Method.

We extract every SMILES-like string inside the thinking block of the
first draw that RDKit parses and that is not a component of the starting
material or reagents, and canonicalize it with RDKit. Structures are
compared by canonical SMILES, so the same molecule written two ways is
not counted as a change. A *change* is a step from one extracted
structure to a different one, and each change is classified by comparing
both structures with the recorded product. Extracted structures include
intermediates and by-products as well as candidate products, so “wrong”
here means “not the recorded product”: wrong$`\to`$wrong changes include
steps through a mechanism, and wrong$`\to`$right means the trace reaches
the recorded product. Consistent with this, among traces with at least
one change the final answer equals the last extracted structure in only
36–69% of cases.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Stage | Condition |     Any  candidate |     $`\geq`$1  change |     Wrong  $`\to`$right |     Right  $`\to`$wrong |     Wrong  $`\to`$wrong |     Final answer  = last cand. |
| S1 | Default | 64.0 | 8.0 | 16.8 | 4.0 | 79.2 | 68.4 |
|  | Consider alternatives | 58.2 | 7.8 | 17.0 | 1.4 | 81.6 | 68.9 |
|  | Think more | 64.3 | 9.6 | 18.2 | 3.3 | 78.6 | 60.7 |
|  | Told wrong | 51.4 | 11.1 | 13.3 | 8.5 | 78.2 | 38.7 |
| S3 | Default | 58.5 | 7.9 | 25.9 | 2.2 | 71.9 | 62.9 |
|  | Consider alternatives | 54.6 | 7.0 | 26.3 | 2.1 | 71.7 | 64.8 |
|  | Think more | 56.7 | 8.4 | 22.5 | 3.0 | 74.5 | 59.0 |
|  | Told wrong | 49.8 | 7.8 | 16.4 | 9.4 | 74.2 | 36.0 |

## Appendix E Statistical methods

#### Comparisons between models or stages.

All models are evaluated on the same 5,000 reactions, so comparisons use
paired tests. For one sample per reaction
(App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B What does each training stage contribute? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
and
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Where do the students beat the teacher? ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning"))
we use McNemar’s test with continuity correction on the discordant pairs
and report paired Wald 95% confidence intervals on the accuracy
difference.

#### Repeated draws.

For the
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Naive test-time scaling after post-training ‣ 4 Results ‣ Distillation, Self-Training, and the Fragility of Learned Chemical Reasoning")
probes with 8 draws per reaction, draws of the same reaction are not
independent. We average within each reaction and test the per-reaction
mean difference across reactions with a two-sided normal ($`z`$) test,
with standard error SD$`/\sqrt{n}`$ over the $`n=5{,}000`$ reactions.
Standard errors are therefore clustered by reaction (0.22–0.25 points
for the reasoning-length prompts).

#### Single-model intervals.

Error bars on single-model accuracy are 95% Wilson score intervals. They
describe uncertainty in one model’s accuracy and are not used to compare
models; overlapping Wilson intervals do not imply equivalence.

#### Multiple comparisons.

Within each family of related tests (the 9 reasoning-length cells; the
12 feedback cells) we report Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted significance
alongside raw $`p`$-values.

#### Training variance.

Each configuration was trained once. Test-set $`p`$-values describe
uncertainty over reactions and sampling, not variation between training
runs.
````
